region: India (the eighteen schools under four Nikāyas)
claim: I-tsing groups the eighteen schools under four chief Nikāyas — the Mahāsāṃghika, the Sthavira, the Mūlasarvāstivāda (his own, 'the Noble Fundamental School which affirms the Existence of All Things', subdivided into Mūlasarvāstivāda, Dharmagupta, Mahīśāsaka and Kāśyapīya), and the Sammitīya. This four-Nikāya frame is the key to reconciling I-tsing's 'Mūlasarvāstivāda' with the plain 'Sarvāstivāda' of Xuanzang's translation.

region: India (the Mūlasarvāstivāda vs the Daśādhyāya / older Sarvāstivāda)
claim: CRITICAL FOR RECONCILIATION: I-tsing distinguishes his Mūlasarvāstivāda from the Daśādhyāya ('Ten Readings', i.e. the older Sarvāstivāda-vinaya). His Record 'resembles generally' the Daśādhyāya, yet he states that the Daśādhyāya 'does not belong to' the Mūlasarvāstivāda. So 'Sarvāstivāda' and 'Mūlasarvāstivāda' are related but NOT identical Vinaya traditions — Xuanzang's plain 'Sarvāstivāda' should therefore be reconciled site by site, not blanket-relabelled as Mūlasarvāstivāda.

source.quote: The Vinaya of the so-called Dasādhyāya (Ten Readings), (though not unlike), does not belong to the Āryamūlasarvāstivāda school.

claim: The three subdivisions of the Mūlasarvāstivāda (Dharmagupta, Mahīśāsaka, Kāśyapīya) do not prevail in India proper, except in three named frontier places — Udyāna, Kharachar (Karashahr) and Kustana (Khotan). This pins specific Mūlasarvāstivāda-subdivision practice to places Xuanzang also describes: Udyāna (Xuanzang entry 38), the Karashahr/Agni region (entry 1), and Gostana/Khotan (entry 145, which Xuanzang calls 'mostly Mahāyāna').

region: India (the four Nikāyas distinguished by practice)
claim: I-tsing distinguishes the four Nikāyas by observable practice rather than doctrine — e.g. the Mūlasarvāstivāda cuts the under-garment skirt straight (the other three schools cut it irregularly), ordains separate rooms in lodgings, and receives food directly into the hand. Such practice-markers are how a school could in principle be identified on the ground.

claim: I-tsing declares that everything in his entire Record is set down in accordance with the Mūlasarvāstivāda and no other school — so his testimony is that of an insider to the very tradition whose name Xuanzang's translation collapses into 'Sarvāstivāda'.

claim: INDICATION OF NĀLANDĀ'S VINAYA: I-tsing lived at Nālandā for ten years and states that his whole Record follows the Mūlasarvāstivāda (obs-019); the discipline he learned and describes there is therefore Mūlasarvāstivāda. He singles out that Nālandā assigns lodging-rooms to the whole assembly of priests every year — one of the distinctive Mūlasarvāstivāda practices (obs-018) — calling it the World-honoured's own teaching. So the ordination/Vinaya tradition of Nālandā (a Mahāyāna doctrinal centre) is, on I-tsing's evidence, the Mūlasarvāstivāda. (Cross-links Xuanzang's Nālandā, entry 82, where Xuanzang names no school.)

source.quote: In the monastery of Nālandā such rules are practised at present; the great assembly of priests assigns rooms every year.

claim: I-tsing's own term throughout the Record is 'Sthavira' (Āryasthaviranikāya); he never writes 'Theravāda'. The work's apparatus equates the Sthavira-nikāya with the Theravāda and with the Vibhajyavāda of Ceylon. So the 'Sthavira' he reports as dominant in South India and universal in Ceylon (obs-004) is the Theravāda/Vibhajyavāda lineage — supporting a 'Sthavira (Theravāda)' bracketing in the reconciliation, with the caveat that modern Theravāda descends specifically from the Sinhalese Mahāvihāra (one of the two Ceylon sects Xuanzang names at Siṃhala, entry 101).
